body: ## Two knockdowns, one stoppage and an unfinished argument

Fabio Wardley has already demonstrated that he can hurt Daniel Dubois. In Manchester on 9 May 2026 he floored the bigger-name puncher in the opening seconds and dropped him again in the third. Yet Dubois eventually became the WBO heavyweight champion, turning the fight into a punishing eleventh-round stoppage. The result was decisive; the route to it was anything but comfortable for the winner. Five months later, they are meeting again at The O2 in London on Saturday 17 October, with Dubois defending the belt he took from Wardley.

That first fight is a better guide to their physical threat than to what happens next. Both camps now know their opponent's best weapon can reach them. The question is not who hits hard. It is which heavyweight can control the moments between the exchanges, stop the other resetting, and avoid giving away the fight after winning individual rounds.
## Tactical key one: the first jab, then the second step

Dubois's strongest sustainable path is to make the jab a positional weapon rather than a scoreboard gesture. If the jab makes Wardley halt his feet and stand square, the right hand becomes more dangerous. But if Dubois paws with his lead hand and steps in without covering the return, Wardley has already shown he can beat him to the punch with a disruptive overhand right. The champion needs a disciplined lead shoulder, a small exit angle after combination punching and enough patience to win minutes rather than hunt one dramatic shot.

Wardley's counter-question is how to make Dubois abandon that structure. His unconventional rhythm and explosive right hand can break a polished sequence. The challenger need not throw more punches than Dubois to win the early phase; he needs to time a few moments when Dubois commits his feet. What Wardley cannot afford is to admire the damage, wait directly in front of Dubois, then take the heavier return fire.
## Tactical key two: Wardley must defend the success he creates

The brutal paradox of May was that Wardley's greatest successes did not keep him safe. He found two knockdowns, yet he could not prevent a prolonged reversal. That points to a rematch plan built around exits after landing, controlling the centre without standing stationary and using the clinch judiciously when Dubois gets his offence moving. A lead of two rounds is not worth much if a fighter must absorb ten more rounds of unbroken punishment to protect it.

A smarter Wardley could throw in short bursts, take a half-step away from Dubois's right-hand lane and change levels on re-entry. That would force Dubois to repeatedly solve new angles. Yet there is a trade-off: too much movement may also suppress Wardley's own chance to punch. His chances improve if he treats power as an opportunity created by timing, rather than an instruction to load up whenever Dubois approaches.
## Tactical key three: what happened after the fourth?

Dubois's recovery in May was not an automatic consequence of being the naturally heavier puncher. He found his rhythm after a horrible start, began imposing sustained offence and steadily increased the physical cost to Wardley. That offers an unusually concrete rematch clue. Wardley must have an answer for the fourth-to-eighth-round phase, when the fight can stop being about a single knockdown and become an argument about stamina, defence and repeated clean punching.

That middle stretch is where we would expect the champion to press his advantage, especially if Wardley's head remains in front of him after combinations. Dubois cannot rely on Wardley tiring at the same rate a second time; rematches are not video replays. But making the challenger fight consistently at Dubois's preferred tempo remains an obvious route towards taking the final rounds out of reach.
## Has the psychological advantage actually changed?

Dangerous heavyweights rarely sound short of confidence during fight week. Dubois has spoken about being less prepared for the first meeting; Wardley publicly challenged that explanation. Those claims are promotional and personal accounts, not something independently established by a medical or conditioning report. The verifiable evidence is what happened in the ring: Dubois was dropped twice and still stopped Wardley, and Wardley was good enough to make the eventual winner's opening rounds very difficult.

Wardley has said he sought the rematch to correct his mistakes. That willingness matters, but only if it produces changes that survive hard contact. A rival already knows he can hurt Dubois; Dubois knows he can finish Wardley. Neither camp needs another motivational speech. They need a cleaner version of the same tactical contest.
## The preparation dispute will be resolved in the ring

Dubois has described being overweight and underprepared for the first encounter, while Wardley has publicly questioned that explanation and discussed the changes in his own training camp. Both accounts are claims made during fight week, not proof of what would have happened in May with different preparation. A more useful question is whether Dubois can protect the first minute of each exchange more consistently, and whether Wardley can keep his defensive shape after landing. Those changes, rather than the rhetoric, will determine whether the rematch differs.
## AURA prediction: Dubois by late stoppage — with a real early danger

Our pick is Daniel Dubois by stoppage between rounds eight and eleven. The logic is cumulative: a more reliably repeatable jab, heavier sustained work as the rounds pass, and direct evidence he can reorganise after Wardley's best success. The pick is not based on assuming Dubois is invulnerable. He was vulnerable twice in May, and one mistimed advance could turn this prediction upside down.

The clearest upset scenario is Wardley scoring early without surrendering his defensive shape afterwards. If he can stay behind a compact guard after the overhand right, change the angle of his retreat and force Dubois to restart his attack again and again, a decision win or a second knockdown sequence becomes possible. We would watch rounds three to six closely: if Dubois is collecting predictable exits and a steady jab, the champion is on course. If Wardley is still creating fresh angles, he is far more than a puncher's chance.
## Where to watch — and a reason to stay for the undercard

The rematch takes place at The O2 in London on Saturday 17 October 2026 and is listed for DAZN pay-per-view in the UK. Broadcast windows are published, but estimated ring walks can change with the supporting bouts; readers should check DAZN's official event guide on fight day rather than treating a prediction as an agreed bell time. Supporting bouts reported for the card include Louie O'Doherty against Michael Gomez Jr and Bakhodir Jalolov against Solomon Dacres.

**Final tactical assessment:** The champion has the stronger late-fight case. The challenger has proved he can create the early crisis. The difference between another thriller and a tactical reversal is not the first knockdown. It is the first minute after it.

body: ## The result was decisive. The next question is more difficult

Osleys Iglesias retained the IBF super-middleweight world title on 8 October in Quebec when Oliver Zaren's corner stopped their contest before the start of round seven. Accounts of the fight describe the Cuban champion steadily increasing the pressure and opening damage around Zaren's eye during the sixth. His team decided there was no benefit in sending him back out. A corner retirement is not a flash knockout, but it can be the clearest expression of sustained dominance.

Iglesias arrived with one of the division's most imposing knockout records. The most revealing element of his rise, however, is not the simple arithmetic of stoppages; it is the way he makes opponents work at a pace they do not choose. A fighter who can strike hard after feinting, pause without surrendering distance and defend after his own attack gives an opponent fewer clean opportunities to reset.
## A southpaw who controls the tempo

The Cuban's southpaw stance creates an inviting route to the straight left against conventional orthodox opponents. But a stance alone wins nothing. Iglesias wants his lead hand to occupy the guard and his feet to define the angle, so his heavier punch arrives when the defender is turning or frozen. His restraint between attacks is what makes the next burst difficult to anticipate.

Zaren was unbeaten before this assignment, and reports indicate he tried to survive the champion's strongest moments by taking hold and slowing the exchanges. That can buy a few seconds; it does not change the basic terms of the fight unless the challenger also answers with his own scoring punches. Once Iglesias could re-establish range, the cost accumulated.
## Power is only half of the examination

A good technician can expose a puncher who needs both feet planted. Iglesias has looked more sophisticated than that. The test for his future challengers is whether they can make him miss twice in the same exchange and then score before he regains his shape. Constant lateral changes, touching the body on entry and stepping out past the lead shoulder may prove more valuable than spending ten rounds behind a motionless high guard.

The opposing temptation is to retreat until there is no ring left. Against a patient, aggressive southpaw, moving straight back buys little if he can keep extending the jab and closing the distance. The most credible strategy would combine controlled movement with intermittent hard counters that make Iglesias respect the cost of coming forward.
## Which rival would answer the real question?

At 168 pounds, the headline names are experienced fighters who can work at several distances and test a champion's defensive recovery. A bout against a technically disciplined elite rival would tell us more about Iglesias than another mismatch arranged to add to a stoppage streak. That is an editorial preference, not an assertion any future contract is signed.

Iglesias should be judged by ring position, the quality of his jab and his decisions when a challenger refuses to panic. Stoppages are excellent theatre; twelve rounds against someone who continually alters the puzzle are often the proof of long-term greatness.
## AURA verdict

The Zaren fight is a significant title defence, not just another entry in a knockout column. Iglesias imposed physical and tactical pressure until the challenger could not continue. His next stage is about the calibre and styles of opposition. The sport will learn more from a difficult challenge than another stoppage whose outcome feels decided beforehand.

body: ## Japan’s rise is not an accident
When Naoya Inoue and Junto Nakatani shared the Tokyo Dome stage, the event could easily be sold as a collision between two exceptional individuals.
That explanation is incomplete.

Japan has become one of the deepest high-level boxing nations in the world, particularly through the lighter divisions. Inoue is the global superstar. Nakatani has built a multi-division championship career. Around them sits a wider system of champions, contenders and technically sophisticated prospects.

The important question is not why Japan produced Inoue. Every country occasionally produces a genius. The important question is why the system keeps producing fighters who look prepared for elite boxing earlier than expected.
## Strong gyms still matter
Japanese boxing remains unusually gym-centred.

The gym is not just where a fighter hires a trainer before camp. It often functions as the long-term sporting institution around the boxer: coaching, matchmaking, management, sparring culture and career development are more closely connected than in many fragmented Western setups.

That continuity matters because technical development in boxing is cumulative. A fighter who spends years inside one coherent system can build habits rather than repeatedly adapting to new voices after each setback.
Elite Japanese gyms also create internal standards. Young fighters see champions training beside them. The distance between prospect and world-class professional becomes physically visible every day.
## The domestic ladder produces meaningful pressure
Japan has long had a structured domestic scene in which national and regional titles carry real developmental value.

That creates fights where a prospect cannot simply rely on a padded unbeaten record. Domestic rivals often know each other, understand the same technical schools and arrive with enough ambition to punish mistakes.
The result is not that every Japanese prospect is rushed. It is that many are asked meaningful questions before the world-title level.
That distinction is crucial.
## Technique is taught to survive pressure, not just look clean
The best Japanese fighters are often praised for textbook fundamentals, but ‘fundamentals’ can sound passive.

Inoue’s balance is devastating because it lets him punch hard without losing position. Nakatani’s long southpaw geometry is dangerous because he can attack from ranges where opponents struggle to answer. Fighters such as Kazuto Ioka built careers from timing, body punching and small positional adjustments rather than athletic spectacle alone.
The common thread is functional technique.
Feet are connected to punching. Defence is connected to counters. Body work is used to change the opponent’s posture. Combinations are thrown with an expectation of return fire.
That is what separates competition-ready technique from gym technique.
## The lower weights are treated as major boxing
One of Japan’s structural advantages is cultural rather than technical: lighter fighters can become real stars.
In some boxing markets, fighters below lightweight struggle for mainstream attention regardless of quality. That reduces promotional investment and can make elite matchups harder to monetise.
Japan does not have the same ceiling.

When smaller fighters can headline major arenas, promoters have a reason to build deep divisions rather than treating them as undercard content. Fans become familiar with the contenders. Rivalries gain value. Young athletes can see a viable professional pathway without needing to become welterweights or heavyweights.
## Inoue changed the international perception
Naoya Inoue did not create Japanese boxing, but he changed how much of the world watches it.

His knockout power solved the traditional marketing problem attached to the lighter divisions. Casual viewers did not need a technical lecture to understand him. Opponents were being hurt by clean, violent punches at the highest level.
Once global attention arrived for Inoue, it became easier for audiences outside Japan to discover Nakatani, Takuma Inoue, Ioka and the next wave beneath them.
That is how one superstar strengthens an ecosystem rather than merely sitting above it.
## Nakatani proved there was more than one
Nakatani’s rise was especially important because it prevented the story becoming ‘Japan has Inoue’.

A tall southpaw with range, timing and serious power, he developed into a champion across multiple divisions and eventually a credible enough threat to make an all-Japanese super-fight internationally significant.
That is the real marker of depth: when a country can produce an opponent good enough to challenge its own global superstar.
## What Britain and America can learn
The lesson is not to copy Japan’s system mechanically. Boxing cultures are too different for that.

But several principles travel well: keep prospects in stable technical environments, give domestic titles real meaning, reward meaningful matchmaking, build stars at every weight and stop treating an unbeaten record as the primary proof of development.
A fighter learns more from ten difficult rounds against a capable domestic rival than from another highlight-reel knockout against someone selected to fall over.
## AURA verdict
Japan’s current strength is not simply a golden generation.
It is what happens when technical culture, gym continuity, competitive domestic boxing and genuine commercial respect for the lighter weights reinforce one another.
Inoue is the masterpiece. Nakatani proved the workshop is still producing.

body: ## Manny Pacquiao is still capable of making boxing stop and look
That fact is both the argument for his return and the reason the sport needs to think carefully about it.

Pacquiao is being discussed for a place on the Tyson Fury–Anthony Joshua event in Cardiff on December 11. A proposed fight with Shakur Stevenson appears to have fallen away, while names including Joe Cordina, Amir Khan and Danny Garcia have circulated around the search for an opponent.

The attraction is obvious. Pacquiao remains one of the most recognisable fighters on earth. Put his name on a major global card and people who have not watched a normal championship show in years will pay attention.
But he is 47.
## The Barrios fight complicated the retirement argument
If Pacquiao had returned against Mario Barrios in 2025 and looked hopelessly slow, this discussion would be easy.
He did not.

After almost four years away, Pacquiao fought the much younger WBC welterweight champion to a majority draw. He was competitive for long stretches, still found angles for the left hand and still possessed enough timing to make a younger champion hesitate.
That performance proved something important: elite skill ages more slowly than reflexes.
It also created a dangerous temptation. Being able to compete is not the same as being insulated from the risks of competing.
## Boxing loves evidence that supports the comeback
Every great older fighter has one performance that makes the next one easier to sell.

George Foreman winning the heavyweight title at 45 remains one of sport’s great stories. Bernard Hopkins kept beating elite opposition into his forties. Pacquiao himself has always been an exception to ordinary athletic expectations.
The problem is that exceptions become marketing templates.

A close fight at 46 can be used to justify another at 47. If that goes well, another can be justified at 48. The line between extraordinary longevity and unnecessary exposure becomes harder to identify because the fighter is still good enough to make the risk look normal.
## Opponent choice matters more than the name on the poster
A fight with Shakur Stevenson would have raised serious concerns because Stevenson is an elite, active, prime-age champion whose speed and precision are among the best in boxing.
A contest with a veteran from Pacquiao’s own era creates a different kind of event. A bout with a smaller fighter moving dramatically through the weights creates another set of questions.
That is why the opponent cannot be selected purely for recognition.
The right matchup has to consider age, natural weight, recent activity and the probability of sustained punishment — not simply whether two famous names fit beneath Fury and Joshua on a poster.
## Is this sport or spectacle?
The honest answer may be both.
Pacquiao’s 2025 performance was legitimate professional competition. It was not an exhibition disguised as a fight. He showed enough to belong in the ring with a world champion that night.

At the same time, his value in Cardiff would come primarily from history. The crowd would be buying the memory of the fighter who moved through eight divisions, overwhelmed champions with impossible angles and became one of the defining athletes of his generation.
There is nothing inherently wrong with nostalgia. Boxing has always sold history.
The responsibility is making sure nostalgia does not become the excuse for a mismatch.
## AURA verdict
Pacquiao has earned the right to be taken seriously when he says he can still fight. His performance against Barrios demands that much.
But the standard for approving another major contest should be higher precisely because of his age.
If he appears in Cardiff, the opponent should be chosen because the fight makes competitive sense now — not because both names once belonged on pound-for-pound lists.
The greatest compliment boxing can pay a legend is not allowing the legend to become bigger than the duty of care around the fight.

body: ## The fight fans want keeps finding another obstacle
Vergil Ortiz Jr. and Jaron ‘Boots’ Ennis have been linked so often that the matchup has started to feel permanent without actually happening.

The latest development moves it farther away again. Oscar De La Hoya says Golden Boy is working on a possible Ortiz fight with former unified welterweight champion Keith Thurman, potentially on a David Benavidez card.
On its own, Ortiz–Thurman is a respectable fight. The problem is what it represents.
## Ortiz needs activity
De La Hoya’s argument is straightforward: Ortiz cannot stay idle while Ennis pursues unification fights.

That is difficult to dispute. Ortiz has already lost valuable time through the contractual dispute that disrupted his career and helped derail earlier Ennis negotiations. A fighter in his physical prime cannot build momentum from press conferences and social-media callouts.
Thurman also gives Ortiz a recognisable name, experience against elite opposition and a style that should force him to solve more than a stationary target.
From a promoter’s perspective, the logic is obvious.
## But boxing careers are full of sensible fights that kill the great fight

The danger is timing. Ennis is chasing belts at junior middleweight, with Josh Kelly and Sebastian Fundora in his orbit. Ortiz has been linked with a move toward middleweight. Every successful fight creates another mandatory, another purse negotiation, another weight-class decision and another reason for the teams to say the timing is wrong.
That is how obvious super-fights disappear.
Ennis has said he still believes the Ortiz fight can happen and has even suggested following him to 160 if necessary. That keeps the rivalry alive. It does not make the logistics easier.
## Is either man ducking?
That word gets used too cheaply.

The record of these negotiations is messy enough that a one-line accusation does not explain it. Ortiz’s dispute with Golden Boy materially affected his ability to make the fight. Ennis has meanwhile prioritised championship consolidation. Both camps have blamed the other at different stages.
A better question is whether the sport is allowing business incentives to overpower competitive urgency.

Fans do not need Ennis and Ortiz to fight because one man is afraid of the other. They need the fight because it is precisely the kind of elite, prime-versus-prime matchup that boxing too often delays until the circumstances have changed.
## What Thurman actually offers Ortiz

At his best, Thurman was an athletic counterpuncher with enough power to make aggressive fighters second-guess their entries. He has also been through championship-level rounds and understands how to change pace.
But this would not be peak Thurman against a developing prospect. Ortiz is now expected to impose himself on a veteran whose best championship years are behind him.

That creates pressure. A narrow or laboured Ortiz win would weaken the argument for treating him as the most dangerous alternative to Ennis. A destructive performance would immediately restart demand for the super-fight.
## The 160-pound problem
Weight may ultimately become the biggest threat to the matchup.

Ortiz has been considering middleweight while Ennis is still collecting titles at 154. If Ortiz establishes himself at 160 and Ennis becomes undisputed at junior middleweight, both men may have legitimate reasons to remain where they are.
The ironic result would be two fighters repeatedly insisting they want each other while building careers that make the meeting progressively less convenient.
## AURA verdict
Ortiz–Thurman is not bad matchmaking. It is understandable matchmaking.
But the Ennis fight should remain the priority because it has something Thurman cannot provide: two unbeaten elite fighters near their primes, with power, speed and genuine uncertainty on both sides.
Boxing should be very careful with the phrase ‘we can make it later’. Later is where too many great fights go to disappear.

body: ## October 9 editorial update
Shakur Stevenson has publicly accepted the proposed 145lb catchweight in talks with Devin Haney. That is an important step, though a final signed agreement has not been announced.
The contest would pit two masters of distance management against one another. Stevenson's subtle counters and Haney's controlling jab could produce a fascinating match of positional discipline.
Weight and physical condition would be essential variables, especially when fighters move away from their habitual divisions.
AURA verdict: this is one of boxing's best potential technical fights. Until contracts are confirmed it remains a negotiation rather than an officially booked event.
## Full original analysis
## A fight boxing has talked around is suddenly becoming real

Shakur Stevenson and Devin Haney have spent years moving through neighbouring divisions, collecting belts and being measured against many of the same elite names. Now the two unbeaten Americans are reportedly in advanced discussions to finally meet.

No deal is signed yet. That distinction matters. Boxing has a long history of turning negotiations into headlines before contracts exist. But the current talks are significant because both fighters are available, both carry major titles in adjacent divisions and both have reached the point where another routine defence would tell us less than this fight would.
The headline is not simply Stevenson versus Haney. The real story is the weight.
## 144 or 147 is not a small detail

Haney is the WBO welterweight champion and has publicly preferred the full 147-pound limit with no rehydration restriction. Stevenson, the WBO champion at 140, has been linked to a 144-pound catchweight.

Three pounds sounds trivial until the fighters involved are elite technicians whose games depend on range, speed and physical control. At 147, Haney is naturally operating in the division he has already chosen and where he beat Brian Norman Jr. to win the title. At 144, Stevenson reduces some of the size and rehydration advantage he would otherwise concede.
That negotiation therefore tells us what each side thinks matters most. Haney wants the fight on welterweight terms. Stevenson wants a bridge between the divisions.
## The tactical argument is more interesting than the unbeaten records
Both men are often described as defensive fighters, but they defend in different ways.

Stevenson’s best work comes from controlling distance before an exchange fully develops. He makes opponents reach, removes the target by inches and is usually balanced enough to answer immediately. His defence is proactive because his feet and lead hand discourage attacks before he has to make dramatic escapes.

Haney is more comfortable using a long jab, clinch control, framing and movement to reset the fight. At his best he forces opponents to start again repeatedly. He is also the larger man here, which could make his jab and physical control more important than pure hand speed.

If the fight is contested closer to 140, Stevenson’s reflexes and compact movement become more attractive. If it is held at the full welterweight limit, Haney’s size, reach and ability to make the contest physically untidy become a bigger part of the equation.
## Who has to take more risks?

Stevenson has spent much of his career making opponents fight his fight. Against Haney, simply waiting may not be enough. Haney is not an undisciplined pressure fighter who will repeatedly overreach just because the crowd grows impatient.
That could force Stevenson to lead more often, step inside behind combinations and accept more moments where he remains in punching range after scoring.

Haney has a different problem. Stevenson is exceptionally difficult to pin down cleanly, and a low-output tactical fight could become a battle over whose single clean shot the judges value more. Haney may need to establish his jab early and make Stevenson feel the difference in size before the fight settles into a fencing match.
## The commercial question has finally caught up with the boxing question
For years the criticism attached to both men has been similar: elite ability, but where is the defining rivalry?
This is the kind of matchup that answers that criticism. It gives Stevenson an opponent with comparable pedigree and gives Haney a chance to beat one of the sport’s most highly rated pure boxers.
The loser would not suddenly become ordinary. In fact, boxing needs more elite fighters willing to risk an unbeaten record against someone capable of beating them.
## AURA verdict
This is one of the best pure boxing matches available in the United States because neither man can rely on a simple physical or stylistic shortcut.
At 147, Haney’s size makes the fight much closer than some Stevenson supporters will admit. At 144, the balance shifts toward Stevenson’s speed, timing and defensive control.
The first battle is therefore happening before the opening bell. Agreeing the weight is not administrative detail. It may be the most important tactical decision either team makes.

body: ## Boxing is approaching a genuine succession fight

Every era eventually reaches the point where the champions remain visible but the sport has already started looking past them. Canelo Álvarez, Oleksandr Usyk, Tyson Fury, Anthony Joshua and the recently retired Terence Crawford have defined much of boxing’s commercial and competitive landscape. The next question is not simply who wins belts after they leave. It is who can become the fighter around whom the sport reorganises itself.
That is a much harder standard than being young, unbeaten or exciting.

Boxing’s unofficial crown is built from several things at once: elite ability, a résumé that survives scrutiny, memorable opponents, activity, personality, market size and the willingness to take fights that create consequences. A fighter can be brilliant and never become the face of the sport. A fighter can also be marketable without ever proving he is the best.

For AURA, the future of boxing therefore has to be judged in tiers. Some fighters are already proven champions entering their prime. Some are one major rivalry away from becoming global stars. Others are still prospects whose potential remains larger than their evidence.
## The throne contenders
### Jaron ‘Boots’ Ennis — the strongest immediate American candidate

Any serious version of this article has to start with Jaron Ennis. The earlier prospect conversation has expired. Ennis is now 36-0 with 32 knockouts, a champion in two divisions and a unified titleholder at junior middleweight.

His June victory over Xander Zayas was important because it supplied something his résumé had often been accused of lacking: a young, unbeaten, ambitious champion who was good enough to create genuine resistance. Zayas buzzed Ennis in the third round. Ennis recovered, adjusted, dropped him three times across the fight and stopped him in the seventh.
That sequence told us more than another easy knockout would have. Ennis can be hurt, remain composed and then regain control against a high-level opponent.

Technically, Boots has perhaps the widest offensive vocabulary among the candidates. He can box orthodox or southpaw, lead or counter, attack the body, work in combination and generate power without turning every exchange into a loading contest. His speed is obvious. The more important quality is how quickly he can move from defence to offence after an opponent commits.
The weakness in the Boots case is not ability. It is event history. The next phase of his career needs opponents whose names matter beyond boxing’s hardcore audience.

That is why Vergil Ortiz Jr matters so much. Ortiz is 24-0 with 22 knockouts and represents the stylistic opposite of Ennis: pressure, physicality, violence and a willingness to force extended exchanges. Ennis-Ortiz is not merely a good fight. It is the kind of rivalry that could define both men.
Unifications with Sebastian Fundora or Josh Kelly would strengthen Ennis’ championship argument. Ortiz could create the star argument.
**AURA position:** Ennis is the clearest candidate to become the next major American pound-for-pound attraction, but he still needs the rivalry that turns excellence into an era.
### Jesse ‘Bam’ Rodriguez — the résumé candidate
Bam Rodriguez is almost mislabelled when he is described as ‘the future’. In competitive terms, much of his future has already arrived.

By 26 he had accumulated elite-level wins across multiple divisions and added another world title by stopping Antonio Vargas. His career already includes victories over Juan Francisco Estrada, Sunny Edwards, Srisaket Sor Rungvisai and Carlos Cuadras.
That is not prospect matchmaking. It is the résumé of a fighter being tested repeatedly against recognised championship quality.

Rodriguez’s boxing is built around geometry rather than spectacle for its own sake. He creates angles after punching, changes levels, attacks the body and rarely follows opponents blindly in straight lines. His pressure is intelligent because his feet position him for the next punch rather than simply moving him closer.

The commercial question is weight. Fighters in the lower divisions have historically had a harder route to becoming boxing’s biggest global attraction. Naoya Inoue has shown that exceptional quality can break that barrier.

That is why the possibility of Bam eventually moving toward Inoue is so significant. A win of that magnitude would not merely add another belt. It could make Rodriguez the central pound-for-pound figure of his generation.
**AURA position:** Rodriguez may have the best chance of finishing this era with the strongest pure boxing résumé, even if becoming the single biggest commercial star remains a different challenge.
### Shakur Stevenson — the technician who needs a defining rivalry

Shakur Stevenson is 25-0 and already a four-division world champion after dominating Teofimo Lopez over twelve rounds. Calling him a prospect would be absurd. The relevant question is whether elite technical control can be converted into the sport’s biggest stage.

Stevenson’s greatest skill is distance management. He does not merely react quickly; he controls where exchanges happen. Opponents regularly find themselves punching from slightly too far away while Stevenson remains close enough to answer.
Against Lopez, he showed that this style can work against a proven, explosive champion at 140 pounds. He did not survive the fight. He controlled it.
The criticism that follows Shakur is commercial rather than technical: will enough people pay to watch a fighter whose primary genius is denying opponents opportunities?
Floyd Mayweather eventually answered that question through enormous rivalries, personality, controversy and elite opponents. Stevenson needs his own version of that ecosystem.
Potential fights involving Devin Haney, Gervonta Davis, Conor Benn or another established attraction could provide the missing emotional stake.

**AURA position:** Shakur may be the purest defensive technician of the group. The remaining test is not whether he can box. It is whether his career can generate the rivalries that make technical brilliance culturally unavoidable.
### David Benavidez — the obvious name prospect lists forget
David Benavidez is often left out of ‘future of boxing’ discussions because he has already spent years near the top. That is exactly why he belongs.

At 29, Benavidez is still young enough to define the post-Canelo period. He is unbeaten, carries a high knockout ratio and has continued climbing in weight rather than waiting for one career-defining opportunity to arrive.

His move through the heavier divisions gives him an important commercial advantage. Bigger fighters generally have access to opponents and narratives that casual audiences understand immediately: size, power and the possibility of heavyweight expansion.
A cruiserweight collision with Jai Opetaia, or a longer-term path toward heavyweight, would give Benavidez the kind of event scale that many smaller fighters have to work much harder to create.

**AURA position:** Benavidez is less ‘next prospect’ than immediate claimant. If he keeps winning against elite names at higher weights, he could become one of the sport’s central attractions before the younger prospects are ready.
## One super-fight away
### Vergil Ortiz Jr — the rival who could become king himself

Ortiz cannot be reduced to ‘the opponent Boots needs’. He is unbeaten, one of the most dangerous punchers around 154 pounds and has shown he can operate in difficult fights rather than only in clean knockout performances.
His appeal is straightforward: pressure creates drama. Ortiz makes opponents work, takes risks to impose his physicality and produces the kind of exchanges that convert first-time viewers into fans.

If he beats Ennis, the entire hierarchy changes. If he loses a classic and wins a rematch, both fighters grow. That is why the matchup carries more historical value than another sequence of mandatory defences.
**AURA position:** Ortiz has a plausible route to the crown because the fight that could make him is already visible.
### Abdullah Mason — the highest-upside young American champion

Abdullah Mason may be the most important name in the truly young category. At 22 he is already a world champion, 21-0 with 18 knockouts, and still several years away from the age usually associated with a fighter’s physical prime.
His offensive talent is easy to recognise: speed, combination punching, a southpaw stance and the confidence to attack openings rather than merely score around them.

But Mason’s development is interesting because it has not been perfectly clean. Being dropped twice by Yohan Vasquez provided useful information. Elite offensive fighters eventually meet opponents who can return fire. The question is whether defensive responsibility develops quickly enough to match the offence.
A unification-level fight against someone such as William Zepeda would tell us far more than another safe defence.
**AURA position:** Mason has perhaps the best combination of youth, power and American-market potential in the sport. His ceiling is enormous, but his defence still has to mature with his ambition.
### Hamzah Sheeraz — size, power and a major-market route
Hamzah Sheeraz belongs in this conversation because he combines physical dimensions, finishing power and access to major British and Middle Eastern audiences.

At super middleweight, he is operating in a division that remains commercially relevant after Canelo. The opportunity is obvious: become the leading figure of the post-Canelo 168-pound landscape rather than simply one of several belt holders.
Sheeraz still needs the sort of elite win that changes how neutral observers discuss him. But if the matchmaking delivers it, his size and power give him a credible path to major-event status.
**AURA position:** not yet at Ennis or Bam’s proven level, but commercially and physically positioned for a major leap.
## The next generation
### Moses Itauma — defeat made the evaluation more honest
The old description of Itauma as an undefeated 20-year-old destroyer is now obsolete. He is 21 and 14-1 after Filip Hrgovic stopped him in the ninth round of their world-title fight.
That loss should not remove him from the future-of-boxing discussion. It should improve the quality of the discussion.

Itauma started quickly, hurt Hrgovic and showed why the excitement existed. Then the fight moved into territory his professional career had rarely required him to solve: an experienced heavyweight surviving the early danger, forcing him to manage energy and continuing to ask questions deep into the fight.

The result exposed pacing, conditioning and late-fight decision-making. Those are real weaknesses at world-title level. They are also developmental weaknesses rather than proof that his speed, power and southpaw skill were imaginary.
The heavyweight division magnifies opportunity. If Itauma rebuilds correctly, a 21-year-old heavyweight with elite hand speed and knockout power remains an extraordinary commercial asset.
**AURA position:** no longer inevitable, still highly relevant. His response to the first defeat is now more important than the unbeaten record ever was.
### Diego Pacheco — the super-middleweight waiting for a signature win

Diego Pacheco has the frame and offensive tools to become a major figure at 168 pounds. At 6ft 4in, he brings dimensions more commonly associated with heavier divisions and has enough power to make that size matter.
The issue is résumé. Potential becomes championship credibility only when it survives an opponent capable of disrupting the plan.
Pacheco’s next major step therefore has to be a fight that can go wrong. If he wins that kind of contest, the conversation changes quickly.
**AURA position:** high ceiling, incomplete evidence.
### Adam Azim — British speed with a world-level question still to answer
Adam Azim is 15-0 with 12 knockouts and has already produced stoppage wins over experienced names including Sergey Lipinets and Steve Claggett.
His hand speed is the headline trait, but the more important development has been his ability to turn speed into controlled aggression rather than simply throwing fast combinations.

The British market gives him access to meaningful domestic rivalries. A fight with Dalton Smith, particularly with championship stakes, would be an ideal separator between prospect excitement and genuine world-level status.
**AURA position:** one of Britain’s best young candidates, but the next opponent matters more than the undefeated number.
### Emiliano Vargas — talent plus the machinery of attention
Emiliano Vargas carries a famous surname, but surname value disappears quickly when a fighter cannot perform. His own development has given the hype more substance.

He has shown genuine offensive talent, finishing ability and an instinct for engaging an audience. That combination matters because becoming the face of boxing has never been purely a technical competition.
The caution is opposition. Vargas needs the level of fighter who forces him to change plans, lose rounds and demonstrate composure.
**AURA position:** strong commercial upside with enough talent to justify serious attention, but still entering the proving phase.
### Xander Zayas — one defeat does not erase a 23-year-old champion
Zayas should remain on the list precisely because Boots beat him.

He entered that fight as a young unified champion and was brave enough to take a dangerous assignment rather than protect his belts against softer opposition. He hurt Ennis in the third round before the more mature fighter took over.
Boxing’s obsession with undefeated records often mistakes a loss for a conclusion. At 23, Zayas has time to treat the defeat as information.
The rebuild will show whether he can tighten the defensive gaps Ennis exploited, improve his ability to control momentum and return to elite opposition without losing ambition.
**AURA position:** downgraded, not dismissed.
## The long-term wildcards
### Curmel Moton

Moton is still a prospect rather than a throne contender. That distinction should be maintained. He has elite-looking reflexes, speed and balance, but those qualities still need to be tested against opponents who can force uncomfortable rounds.
The attraction is his age. At 20, he has time to build properly rather than rush toward comparisons with fighters who already own world titles.
### Bruce Carrington

Carrington’s status has changed from prospect to champion. Technical polish, timing and composure have carried him to a title, but featherweight greatness requires marquee unifications and opponents who can broaden his audience.
### Callum Walsh

Walsh has one of the more interesting crossover profiles in the sport: an aggressive southpaw style, an Irish-American fan base and growing visibility through the new promotional landscape. What he needs now is a sequence of opponents who transform that popularity into boxing credibility.
### Keyshawn Davis

Davis remains one of the more naturally gifted American fighters of his age group, but career momentum is not permanent. The next phase has to include a major opponent and a clear championship route. Talent keeps him in the discussion; decisions around opposition determine how long he stays there.
## Why rivalries matter more than rankings
The sport often asks who the next Canelo or Mayweather will be as though one fighter simply inherits a vacant office.
That is not how boxing history usually works.

Leonard became Leonard partly because Hearns, Duran and Hagler existed. Ali needed Frazier and Foreman. Pacquiao’s rivalry with Márquez added depth to both men’s legacies. Mayweather’s era was amplified by the long-running argument around Pacquiao.
The next king of boxing probably needs an enemy.

Ennis has Ortiz. Bam has the possibility of Inoue. Stevenson needs the opponent who turns his technical supremacy into a cultural argument. Mason needs another young champion to grow alongside him. Itauma eventually needs a heavyweight rival his own generation can claim.
Without those fights, boxing risks producing several excellent champions and no defining era.
## So who is actually closest to the crown?
If the question is who is closest right now, Jaron Ennis has the strongest combination of prime age, knockout power, American market potential and upward competitive trajectory.
If the question is whose résumé may eventually look best, Bam Rodriguez has an extraordinary head start.
If the question is pure technical control, Shakur Stevenson belongs near the top of any discussion.
If the question is highest upside among the youngest champions, Abdullah Mason is difficult to ignore.
If the question is commercial scale through bigger weight classes, David Benavidez may have the clearest immediate opportunity.
And if boxing wants another heavyweight phenomenon, Moses Itauma remains alive in that race — but now he has to prove he can learn.
## AURA verdict
The future of boxing is not one prospect list. It is a succession battle.

Boots Ennis is our current lead candidate because he combines elite ability, finishing power, championship achievement and a visible path to the rivalry that could make him a genuine superstar. Bam Rodriguez may become the generation’s most accomplished boxer. Shakur Stevenson already has the technical credentials. Benavidez has the size and event potential. Abdullah Mason has youth on his side.
But none of them should be crowned on projection alone.
The throne will be decided by who takes the fights, beats the rivals and gives the sport nights people remember.
Talent creates contenders. Rivalries create kings.

articles.title: Does Anthony Joshua really have a glass jaw?
articles.summary: Joshua has been dropped and stopped often enough for the phrase to follow him everywhere. But punch resistance, recovery and decision-making under fire are not the same thing.

sources.name: BBC Sport — Joshua vs Ruiz I
MMA Fighting — Fury vs Joshua date and location

image.alt: Anthony Joshua and Kristian Prenga exchange punches during their July 2026 heavyweight fight in Jeddah
image.credit: Matchroom Boxing / Getty Images via MMA Fighting
image.caption: Joshua was dropped twice by Kristian Prenga before recovering to win in round two.

body: ## Boxing’s easiest diagnosis
Anthony Joshua gets hurt and the phrase appears immediately: glass jaw.

It is one of boxing’s most convenient labels because it compresses several different questions into two words. Can a fighter absorb the initial punch? How quickly does he recover? What decisions does he make while hurt? Can he deny an opponent the follow-up? Those are connected qualities, but they are not identical.
Joshua’s history gives both sides of the argument plenty of material.
## Klitschko is inconvenient evidence for the prosecution
Wladimir Klitschko dropped Joshua heavily in the sixth round at Wembley in 2017. Joshua got up, survived the crisis and stopped Klitschko in the eleventh.

That matters because a truly simplistic ‘one good punch and he is finished’ explanation does not fit the night. Joshua absorbed a major right hand from one of the most accomplished heavyweight punchers of his generation and recovered sufficiently to win.

It also showed the pattern that would follow him. When Joshua is badly hurt, his performance can change dramatically. His feet become less dependable, his defensive choices become more urgent and the opponent is suddenly invited into a different fight.
## Ruiz created the label

The first Andy Ruiz Jr fight in 2019 transformed that vulnerability into a public identity. Joshua dropped Ruiz, attacked to finish and was then caught himself. Ruiz’s fast combinations repeatedly found him before the contest ended in the seventh round.

The important detail is that Joshua was not simply rendered unconscious by the first damaging punch. He was hurt, remained in the contest and then struggled to recover while Ruiz kept applying pressure.
That points toward a more useful concept than ‘glass’: recovery under sustained attack.
## Dubois strengthened the case

Daniel Dubois dropped Joshua multiple times before stopping him in the fifth round in 2024. There is no reason to minimise that defeat. Joshua was repeatedly available for clean heavyweight punches and the final right hand ended the fight emphatically.
But heavyweight boxing has to be judged in heavyweight context. A clean shot from an elite heavyweight can stop a fighter without proving that his chin is uniquely defective.

The technical question is why the shot landed and what happened after the earlier damage. Positioning, defensive responsibility after punching and the ability to reset under pressure matter as much as an abstract rating of somebody’s chin.
## Then Prenga made the argument weird again
In July 2026 Kristian Prenga dropped Joshua twice in the opening round. The upset appeared to be unfolding in real time.
Joshua came back out for the second round, increased his aggression and stopped Prenga at 2:43.

That six-minute sequence contains the entire Joshua debate. He was vulnerable enough to be floored twice by an opponent he was expected to beat. He was also capable of recovering, reorganising and producing the decisive punch one round later.
A completely shattered chin is a poor explanation for both events happening in the same fight.
## Chin, recovery and survival

Punch resistance describes the ability to take the initial impact. Recovery describes how quickly balance, awareness and physical control return. Survival craft describes what a fighter does during the interval between being hurt and being safe again.
Joshua’s vulnerability may be better understood across the second and third categories than through the first alone.

Some fighters instinctively clinch, move their head off line, step away from the opponent’s strongest hand and burn seconds. Joshua has sometimes remained available for follow-up attacks while compromised. That can make the original punch look more decisive than it was because the damage compounds.
This is technical analysis from fight evidence, not a medical diagnosis of Joshua’s neurological response.
## Why Fury makes the question important
Tyson Fury does not need to possess Deontay Wilder’s one-shot power for Joshua’s recovery to matter on December 11. Fury can change rhythm, work at range and use his size in prolonged exchanges.

If Joshua is hurt, the critical phase may be the next thirty seconds rather than the punch itself. Can he create a clinch on his own terms? Can he leave the line without backing straight up? Can he make Fury reset instead of allowing the next attack to begin immediately?
That is where the fight could be decided.
## AURA verdict
Anthony Joshua is hittable and has demonstrated real vulnerability when badly hurt. Pretending otherwise would ignore too much evidence.
But ‘glass jaw’ is too crude to explain a fighter who survived Klitschko, completed long elite-level fights and recovered from two knockdowns against Prenga to win moments later.
The sharper criticism is this: Joshua’s recovery and survival decisions have sometimes failed him after the first damaging shot.
That is still a weakness. It is simply a more accurate one.

articles.title: Is Moses Itauma a hype job? The real test starts after the loss
articles.summary: Filip Hrgovic stopped the 21-year-old in a world-title fight. That ended Itauma’s unbeaten record, not the argument over how good he can become.

sources.name: RTÉ — Itauma loses to Hrgovic
Bad Left Hook — Hrgovic reflects on the win
Bad Left Hook — pre-fight step-up analysis

body: ## Boxing loves building gods. It loves destroying them even more.
Before August 29, Moses Itauma was one of the sport’s favourite predictions: future heavyweight champion, elite prospect, perhaps the young man ready to inherit a division dominated by older names.
Then Filip Hrgovic stopped him in the ninth round at The O2 and won the vacant IBF heavyweight title.
Within minutes the vocabulary changed. Exposed. Overrated. Hype job.
But what exactly did the fight expose?
## Start with what actually happened

Itauma was not outclassed from the opening bell. He started quickly, used his speed and dropped Hrgovic in the second round. He built a lead and made the experienced Croatian absorb sustained punishment.
Hrgovic kept coming.
That became the problem.

The fight moved into territory Itauma’s professional career had rarely forced him to explore: an experienced heavyweight surviving the early damage, remaining dangerous and asking the young fighter to make good decisions while fatigue accumulated.

By the later rounds the energy equation had changed. Hrgovic had experience operating while tired. Itauma did not have the same bank of professional rounds to draw from. In the ninth, Hrgovic broke through and the contest was stopped at 2:27.
That is a defeat. It is not evidence that everything seen before it was imaginary.
## The hype was incomplete, not invented
Itauma’s reputation was built around qualities visible immediately: speed, southpaw angles, combination punching, power and unusual composure for his age.
Hrgovic did not erase those qualities. He exposed areas that highlight reels could not prove.

Pacing. Energy management. Patience when a finish does not arrive. Defence while tired. The ability to accept that an opponent has survived the best sequence and return to structured boxing instead of continually trying to force the ending.
Those are serious gaps at world-title level.
They are also trainable.
## The problem with the Tyson comparison
Young knockout-producing heavyweights inevitably attract comparisons with Mike Tyson, especially when discussion turns to records for becoming champion at a young age.
That creates a dangerous countdown mentality. How fast did he knock the opponent out? How quickly can he reach a title? Why wait?
The Hrgovic fight supplied the answer boxing rarely enjoys hearing: because development requires experiences that cannot be scheduled after the championship.
Itauma reached a world-title fight at 21. He discovered a problem he had not yet solved. That is what high-level sport is supposed to do.
## Losing at 21 should not be a crisis

Boxing’s obsession with undefeated records distorts development. A footballer can fail in major matches at 21 and still become world class. A tennis player can lose repeatedly while building an elite career. In boxing, a single defeat is often treated as proof that every previous win was fraudulent.
That is commercially understandable and competitively absurd.
Itauma’s loss becomes damaging only if his team responds badly to the information it provided.
## What should happen next

The wrong response would be immediate revenge simply to prove the loss meant nothing. It clearly meant something. The other wrong response would be two years of harmless opponents designed only to restore a shiny record.
The next stage should be developmental matchmaking.
First, a durable heavyweight expected to survive the early attack. Itauma needs rounds in which the knockout is unavailable and winning requires disciplined pacing.
Second, a physical pressure fighter who will make the fight uncomfortable: clinches, body work, contested space and moments where Itauma has to regain structure.
Third, another contender once those improvements are visible.
The goal is not to protect Itauma from questions. It is to keep asking useful ones.
## Should Hrgovic be the destination?
A rematch can become a major fight because the first contest produced a clear tactical story. Itauma had success early. Hrgovic survived, extended him and took over late.
For Itauma to make a rematch meaningful, he should first demonstrate answers to the questions Hrgovic created.

Can he fight economically when the opponent refuses to fall? Can he maintain defensive shape after eight hard rounds? Can he recognise when chasing a knockout is costing more energy than it is creating damage?
If those answers change, the rematch changes.
## AURA verdict
Moses Itauma is no longer an unbeaten phenomenon. That may ultimately be useful.
Hrgovic gave him more developmental information in nine rounds than another sequence of early knockouts could have supplied. The talent looked real. So did the gaps.
Calling him a hype job at 21 misunderstands both the fight and the purpose of development.
The hype is finished. Now the career gets interesting.

articles.title: The most powerful people in boxing aren’t boxers
articles.summary: No commissioner owns boxing. Money, broadcasters, promoters, sanctioning bodies and fighter relationships all control different pieces. AURA maps where the real power sits.

sources.name: LegalClarity — boxing power structure
MMA Fighting — UFC role in Fury vs Joshua

image.caption: Turki Alalshikh and Dana White represent two of the most influential forces reshaping modern boxing.

body: ## Nobody owns boxing
That is the first fact required to understand the sport.

There is no NFL-style league office, no single commissioner controlling the schedule and no central table determining who must fight whom. Professional boxing is a network of independent fighters, managers, promoters, sanctioning bodies, broadcasters, regulators, venues and financiers.
Power therefore belongs to whoever can make the other pieces move.
## Power centre one: capital

Recent boxing has demonstrated the obvious advantage of controlling the budget. A sufficiently valuable financial offer can bring promotional rivals together, persuade elite fighters to accept risk and create events whose economics would be difficult to reproduce through tickets and pay-per-view alone.

That is why Turki Alalshikh has occupied such a central position in contemporary boxing. Boxing News placed him at the centre of its 2026 discussion of influence, pointing to Riyadh Season events, international shows and the wider network around The Ring and Zuffa Boxing.
Capital does not decide who wins. It frequently decides which fights become realistic.
## Power centre two: distribution
A fight nobody can watch has limited commercial value. Broadcasters and streaming platforms therefore hold a second form of power: access to the audience.

DAZN’s investment in boxing reshaped promotional relationships. Netflix’s move into major live events adds another kind of buyer—one capable of valuing a fight as a global cultural moment rather than only as a traditional pay-per-view product.
The platform can increasingly influence the scale, presentation and timing of the event.
## Power centre three: promoters

Promoters remain essential because fighters are not interchangeable inventory. The relationship between an athlete and the team guiding his career carries trust, contractual rights, market knowledge and negotiating leverage.
Eddie Hearn, Frank Warren and other established promoters can bring major names to the table. That remains power.
What has changed is that bringing the fighter no longer guarantees ownership of every other part of the show.
## Power centre four: sanctioning bodies
The WBA, WBC, IBF and WBO control recognised world titles and mandatory structures. That gives them leverage over championship pathways.
A mandatory challenger can force a negotiation or purse bid. A title can be stripped. A vacant belt can redirect an entire division.
The bodies do not own the fighters, but their decisions can change the market around them.
## Power centre five: the fighter
The biggest fighters can override almost every structure above because the event does not exist without them.

Anthony Joshua’s public loyalty to Eddie Hearn during the Fury promotion is a useful example. When a fighter has enough commercial value, his preference about who represents him matters to financiers and platforms.
At the very top of the sport, star power can become negotiating power.
Below that level, the balance changes rapidly.
## Why the current system feels unstable

Each power centre wants a different thing. The fighter wants money, opportunity and control. The promoter wants a sustainable business and valuable contracts. The broadcaster wants audience. The sanctioning body wants its title represented. The financier may want global visibility or strategic value beyond one event.
A great fight happens when those interests align.
A delayed fight happens when they do not.

This is why boxing can simultaneously appear chaotic and incredibly flexible. The absence of central authority causes fragmentation, but it also allows unusual coalitions to form when the incentive is large enough.
## AURA verdict
The most powerful person in boxing can change depending on the question.
Who controls the money? Who controls the fighter? Who controls the belt? Who controls the screen? Who can place all four in the same room?
That last ability may be the most important form of power in the modern sport.
Boxing is not ruled from one office. It is ruled by negotiation.

articles.title: Sebastian Fundora: the Towering Inferno who fights against type
articles.summary: At 6ft 6in and 154 pounds, Sebastian Fundora should be a long-range puzzle. Instead, one of boxing’s strangest champions often chooses violence at close quarters.

Boxing Social — Fundora after Thurman
WBC — Fundora vs Hadribeaj

image.alt: Sebastian Fundora in boxing trunks and gloves with Keith Thurman after their bout in the ring
image.credit: Associated Press / WSLS — archival boxing photograph
image.caption: Sebastian Fundora and Keith Thurman after their March 2026 fight; an archival ringside photograph.

body: ## October 9 editorial update
Fundora's unusual height is only half the story. His willingness to exchange at close range can negate the usual advantage of a long jab.
Opponents must keep angles on their exits, target the body and stop him from sustaining work once they reach the pocket.
The scheduled October 17 Ermal Hadribeaj challenge offers another measure of those tactics, with Fundora's ring positioning and defensive discipline under scrutiny.
AURA verdict: the best solution is to make Fundora reset rather than simply try to get inside his reach.
## Full original analysis
## Boxing is not supposed to produce fighters shaped like this

Sebastian Fundora is 6ft 6in and competes at 154 pounds. That sentence alone explains why opponents have to prepare for something unusual. The obvious instruction for a boxer with that frame would be simple: stay tall, use the jab, make shorter men cross dangerous ground and punish them on the way in. Fundora can do that. The strange part is that he often chooses not to.

Fundora has built his reputation by turning an extraordinary physical advantage into a style that can look almost wilfully contradictory. He is comfortable at range, but he is also willing to stand close, trade hooks and uppercuts and make fights ugly. That is why the nickname ‘The Towering Inferno’ fits better than a conventional description of a tall boxer. The height is obvious. The inferno is the choice.
## The reach advantage he keeps giving back

For shorter opponents, the normal tactical problem is getting through the end of the jab. Against Fundora, that problem can suddenly disappear because he is prepared to meet them in the pocket. It looks reckless, but there is logic beneath it. His length does not vanish at close range. Long arms can create unusual uppercut and hook trajectories, while his height can make opponents punch upward for extended periods.

The cost is that inside exchanges also remove the safety his dimensions could provide. Fundora can be hit. He has been dropped. He has lost. His fights therefore carry an element many technically gifted champions try to eliminate: uncertainty.
That uncertainty is part of his appeal. Fundora does not ask the audience to admire geometry from a distance for twelve rounds. He regularly lets an opponent believe the fight is available to them.
## Tszyu changed the scale of the story

Fundora’s 2024 win over Tim Tszyu transformed him from an unusual contender into a world champion. The fight was chaotic, bloody and difficult to reduce to a clean tactical narrative. It also established that Fundora could operate under the pressure of a major championship contest and survive a fight that did not unfold neatly.

The WBC says he has since made three successful defences of the title, including a rematch with Tszyu. He now enters an October 17 defence against unbeaten Ermal Hadribeaj with a 24-1-1 record and 16 knockouts.

That record matters, but so does the way he has accumulated it. Fundora is not undefeated and therefore does not carry the fragile marketing burden of protecting a zero. He has already experienced a knockout defeat, rebuilt and reached championship level afterwards. That can free a fighter psychologically. The worst headline has already happened.
## Why his style is difficult to copy

A fighter’s physical dimensions can be imitated in sparring only approximately. Finding someone who is both exceptionally tall for the division and willing to fight inside is even harder. An opponent might recruit a rangy sparring partner to replicate the jab, then a pressure fighter to reproduce the close exchanges. Neither alone gives the complete picture.

Fundora also forces awkward changes in punching height. Straight shots rise toward his head. Body punches can leave a shorter fighter underneath long counters. Clinch positions feel different because shoulders, elbows and leverage arrive from unusual angles.
None of that makes him unbeatable. It makes preparation less familiar.
## The question at 154

The super-welterweight division is full of technically capable fighters. The challenge is identifying the style that can consistently punish Fundora for abandoning distance without being overwhelmed once the exchanges begin.

A disciplined boxer might try to make him pay every time he steps inside. A pressure fighter might welcome the invitation and attack the body. A puncher may simply accept the risk and bet that Fundora’s willingness to trade eventually creates one clean opportunity.
The problem is that Fundora has now seen several versions of those ideas. Experience is beginning to catch up with his physical advantages.
## AURA verdict

Fundora is interesting because he does not fight the way a textbook tells us a 6ft 6in super-welterweight should fight. If he simply stayed outside, he might be easier to explain. Instead he turns a rare body type into a deliberately chaotic style.

That contradiction is his identity. Boxing gave him the dimensions of a heavyweight, the weight limit of a super-welterweight and the instincts of a fighter who often wants to meet you in the middle. The result is one of the sport’s most distinctive champions.

articles.title: Boxing won the lottery. What happens when the Saudi money stops?
articles.summary: Saudi-backed investment helped remove barriers that kept major fights apart. The uncomfortable question is whether boxing has now reset its economics around money that may not always be available.

sources.name: Boxing News Power 50
Queensberry — 2024 review

image.alt: Artur Beterbiev and Dmitry Bivol face off with their world-title belts before their Riyadh fight
image.credit: Mark Robinson / Matchroom Boxing / Getty Images, via MMA Fighting
image.caption: Beterbiev–Bivol became a flagship example of the elite matchups enabled by Saudi-backed boxing investment.

body: ## The problem boxing always said it had

For decades, supporters were told some version of the same sentence: the fight is too difficult to make. Different promoters. Different broadcasters. Different advisers. Different financial expectations. Too much risk for one side and not enough reward for the other.

Saudi-backed boxing did not eliminate every political problem, but it changed the arithmetic. Fury fought Usyk. Beterbiev fought Bivol. Promotional rivals appeared on the same cards. Events were built around sporting ambition that conventional pay-per-view economics might have struggled to support at the same scale.
That deserves acknowledgement. But success creates its own dependency.
## The new price of a big fight

Once fighters, promoters and managers see what can be paid for a major event, that number enters future negotiations. A purse is not experienced in isolation. It becomes a reference point. If a boxer earned an exceptional amount for one difficult contest, the next opponent is unlikely to negotiate as though that night never happened.
This is where the Saudi era may have changed boxing more deeply than the individual fights themselves. It did not simply fund events. It may have reset expectations about what elite risk should cost.
That is manageable while a buyer exists with reasons to value the event beyond ordinary gate receipts and pay-per-view calculations. It becomes harder if that buyer becomes more selective.
## The warning signs are not the same as an exit

Recent reporting has raised questions about a broader shift toward financial sustainability in Saudi sport and about Turki Alalshikh’s own future involvement. That does not prove that investment in boxing is about to disappear. It does make sustainability a legitimate subject rather than a hypothetical one.

Boxing should distinguish between less spending and no spending. A more selective model could still stage major fights while demanding clearer commercial logic. The consequences would depend on which events continue to receive support and which are returned to conventional market economics.
## What Saudi backing actually solved
The most important achievement was not luxury production. It was alignment.

A promoter who normally competes with another promoter could participate in a shared card because the event itself offered enough value. Fighters could accept difficult opposition because the reward compensated for the risk. Broadcasters could attach themselves to occasions with obvious global relevance.
Money turned fragmented interests toward the same destination.
That is why the biggest legacy question is whether the cooperation survives if the exceptional incentives shrink.
## Could boxing go back?

Not easily. Once a market has experienced higher prices, lower prices feel like cuts even when they are commercially rational. Fighters may wait for better offers. Promoters may delay risky matchups. Broadcasters may become more cautious. The old politics can return quickly when every participant again has to protect a smaller pool of revenue.

There is also a fan problem. Audiences have now seen what happens when the sport behaves as though the best should fight the best. Returning to years of marination would feel even less acceptable than it did before.
That is why the current era creates pressure on boxing to learn rather than merely spend.
## The opportunity hidden inside the risk

If the sport uses this period to normalise cross-promotional deals, improve global distribution and build events around competitive quality, then the money may leave behind infrastructure and habits that remain valuable.
If it does not, the industry may discover that it rented cooperation rather than built it.

The ideal outcome is not permanent dependence on one source of capital. It is a healthier market in which promoters have learned that collaboration can be profitable, broadcasters understand the value of global events and fighters no longer need an unbeaten record protected for years before taking a genuine risk.
## AURA verdict

Saudi investment has been good at answering boxing’s oldest excuse: ‘we cannot make the fight.’ The next challenge is harder. Can boxing continue making those fights when the financial conditions are less extraordinary?
The sport won the lottery. The smartest thing it can do now is build something with the winnings.

articles.title: The promoter is dying — or boxing is changing what a promoter is
articles.summary: Hearn, Warren and the classic promotional model are not disappearing. But capital, streaming platforms and new event operators are moving power around the sport.

MMA Mania — Hearn and White meeting
Boxing News Power 50

image.caption: Dana White’s move into boxing has intensified the argument over who controls the modern event.

body: ## October 9 editorial update
Streaming platforms and major promoters increasingly compete to own the audience relationship as much as the fight itself.
The DAZN and Netflix distribution models, together with Zuffa's ambitions, raise questions about who controls fighter exposure and broadcast presentation.
The Hearn–White fight over production and promotional roles illustrates why contractual control has become so visible to fans.
AURA verdict: boxing benefits from investment only when it leads to better matchmaking, credible coverage and a clearer product for supporters.
## Full original analysis
## The old job description

The traditional boxing promoter did almost everything that mattered outside the ropes. Sign the fighter. Build the local audience. Negotiate the television deal. Secure the venue. Sell the tickets. Control the press conference. Protect the relationship with sanctioning bodies. Then, when the fighter became valuable enough, negotiate with a rival promoter.
That model still exists. Eddie Hearn and Frank Warren remain major operators. But the structure around them is changing.

The clearest sign is Fury–Joshua. The fight involves established promoters, Saudi-linked backing, Netflix distribution and a public dispute over Dana White and UFC’s production or promotional role. It is not simply one promoter putting on one show.
## Capital has moved upstream

In the classic model, the promoter raised or risked the money and then tried to recover it through tickets, media rights and sponsorship. In the newer model, a powerful capital partner or platform can begin with the desired event and assemble the pieces underneath it.
That changes leverage.

If the person controlling the budget can bring rival promoters into the same room, the promoter becomes one important participant rather than the sole architect. The fighter relationship still matters. Local expertise still matters. But neither automatically guarantees control of the entire event.
## Streaming changed the broadcaster too

Television networks once needed regular boxing inventory. Promoters could build long relationships around that demand. Global streamers can think differently. They may value a small number of huge live events more than a weekly boxing schedule.
That favours event-led thinking. Instead of asking which promoter’s stable fills the next twelve dates, the platform can ask which single fight creates the biggest global moment.
The promoter then competes not only with another promoter, but with the possibility that the platform, financier and production partner can assemble an event around the fighters themselves.
## Dana White is the symbol, not the entire story
White attracts attention because UFC represents the opposite of boxing’s fragmentation: one dominant brand, central matchmaking, central rankings and a more controlled promotional ecosystem.
Zuffa Boxing’s arrival therefore carries an implicit argument. Boxing does not merely need another promoter; it may need a different operating system.

That is why the Hearn–White feud is more interesting than the insults. Hearn represents an exceptionally successful version of the traditional boxing promoter. White represents a model built around centralised control. Their disagreement is partly personal and partly structural.
## Why promoters still matter

It would be premature to declare the promoter obsolete. Fighters still need advocates who understand their market, career position and contractual value. Local promotion remains essential for building prospects. Relationships with venues, commissions, sponsors and media do not appear automatically because a large platform has money.

Promoters also carry something algorithms and capital cannot easily manufacture: trust with fighters. When Anthony Joshua publicly backs Eddie Hearn during a dispute, that relationship has commercial value.
The role is therefore more likely to evolve than disappear.
## From owner of the show to specialist partner
The future promoter may look less like the owner of every part of an event and more like a specialist within a larger coalition.

One party provides capital. Another owns the media platform. Another handles production. A promoter brings the fighter and market expertise. A sanctioning body supplies the title framework. A venue partner supplies the building and local operation.
That structure is messier than a single league, but it is already visible.
## AURA verdict
The promoter is not dying. The monopoly over promotion is.

The people who survive will be the ones comfortable sharing control when sharing control produces a bigger event. Hearn, Warren, White and the next generation are not competing for the same job description anymore.
They are competing to define what the job becomes.

articles.title: The belts don’t tell you who the best fighter is anymore
articles.summary: Four major sanctioning bodies, separate rankings and secondary titles can leave casual fans asking a basic question boxing should answer easily: who is actually number one?

sources.name: Boxing OS — sanctioning bodies explained
